notes.meaning: Hoshea became the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel, ruling from the capital city of Samaria for nine years. He had taken power by killing the previous king during a time of great political chaos. His official rule was finally established in the twelfth year of King Ahaz of Judah.

Hoshea did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, though he was not as bad as the kings who came before him. He did not force the people to worship idols, and he allowed them to travel to Jerusalem to worship if they wanted. Even so, small improvements in behavior could not undo centuries of national rebellion against God.

King Shalmaneser of Assyria invaded Israel and forced Hoshea to submit to his rule. Hoshea had to become his servant and pay heavy tribute money each year to stay in power. Leaning on foreign powers instead of trusting God brought Israel into bitter slavery.

Hoshea plotted against Assyria by sending messengers to make a military deal with the king of Egypt. He also stopped paying his required yearly tribute to Assyria. When the Assyrian king discovered this betrayal, he captured Hoshea and threw him into prison.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars debate the identity of King So, suggesting the name may refer to Pharaoh Osorkon IV, Pharaoh Piankhy, or the Egyptian capital city of Sais.

notes.meaning: The Assyrian army swept across the entire land of Israel and surrounded Samaria, cutting off all food and supplies for three years. The city had strong fortifications, so the people held out as long as they could. A long siege was a slow and agonizing way for a city to fall.

Samaria finally fell to the Assyrians, marking the total end of the northern kingdom of Israel. The conquerors marched the Israelites far away from their homeland and resettled them across the Assyrian Empire in places like Halah, the Habor River region, and Medite cities. This mass deportation was meant to crush their culture so they would never rebel again.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Assyrian records state that King Sargon II completed the capture of Samaria in 722 BC, likely serving as military commander when Shalmaneser V died during the siege.

notes.meaning: Israel fell not just because Assyria was powerful, but because the people had sinned against the Lord their God. The Lord had lovingly rescued their ancestors from slavery under Pharaoh in Egypt. In return for His great mercy, the people turned their backs on Him and worshiped false gods.

The Israelites adopted the evil customs of the Canaanites, the very nations God had driven out of the promised land centuries earlier. They also obeyed the sinful religious laws created by their own kings, such as worshiping golden calves. Instead of living as a holy example to the world, they copied the pagan culture around them.

The people secretly did wrong things against God, foolishly acting as if He could not see what was done in private. They built pagan shrines called high places in every settlement, from remote watchtowers out in the fields to large walled cities. We fool ourselves when we imagine our secret sins are hidden from God.

The Israelites set up carved stone pillars and wooden Asherah poles dedicated to Canaanite fertility goddesses. They placed these idols on top of every hill and under every shady green tree. They filled their land with symbols of false religion instead of honoring the God who created nature.

They burned incense at these pagan shrines just like the Canaanite nations God had cast out before them. Incense was meant for holy prayer to the true God, but they offered it to worthless idols. Their wicked behavior provoked the Lord's righteous anger against their unfaithfulness.

The people served lifeless statues even though the Lord had clearly commanded them, 'You shall not do this thing.' The biblical writers used insulting words for these idols to show they were as filthy and useless as piles of dung. Disobeying God's direct commands always brings spiritual ruin.

God did not punish His people without warning, but patiently sent prophets and seers to both Israel and Judah. These messengers urged the people to turn from their evil ways and obey the Law given through Moses. God's warnings were an act of patient love, giving them many chances to repent.

The people refused to listen and stiffened their necks, acting like stubborn oxen that refuse to bow to a master's yoke. They repeated the same stubborn rebellion as their ancestors who died in the desert because they did not trust God. When people refuse to trust God, their hearts become hard toward His truth.

They rejected God's laws, broke the sacred covenant agreement He had made with their ancestors, and ignored all His warnings. By chasing after empty, worthless idols, they became empty and worthless themselves. People always end up becoming like whatever they choose to worship.

The Israelites tossed aside every commandment of God and made two metal calves to worship at Dan and Bethel. They built Asherah poles, bowed down to the sun, moon, and stars, and served the pagan god Baal. One compromise led to another until their worship looked completely like the heathen nations around them.

The people sank into terrible cruelty by burning their own sons and daughters in the fire as sacrifices to idols. They also used fortune-telling and magic, completely selling themselves to do evil in God's sight. Sin blinds people until the most awful wickedness seems acceptable to them.

The Lord was deeply angered by Israel's constant unfaithfulness, so He banished them from the land where His presence and blessing dwelt. The entire northern kingdom was wiped away into exile, leaving only the southern kingdom of Judah behind. Being cut off from God's favor is the greatest disaster that can happen to any nation.

Even the southern tribe of Judah failed to keep the commands of the Lord their God. Instead of learning from Israel's tragic downfall, Judah copied the very same idolatrous customs that Israel had invented. Bad examples can easily lead others astray when people stop watching their own hearts.

Because of their rebellion, the Lord rejected all the descendants of Israel and brought great suffering on them. He handed them over to invading armies to be plundered until He finally drove them out of His presence into foreign exile. God is faithful to His word, which includes the sure consequences of turning away from Him.
